subChunks.title: Services Grid
subChunks.hookHtml: The header holds attention. The hero earns trust. Now the site must communicate value. The services section answers the visitor's primary question: "What do they actually do?" Three cards. Clear hierarchy. And a hover interaction that rewards attention — a technique that requires Tailwind's most powerful compositional pattern: group and group-hover:.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator: "The hover on this card has to feel alive. When the card lifts, the icon changes colour. Not because the icon is hovered — because the card is. This is the group pattern. The parent watches. The child reacts. It is the difference between a UI that feels built and one that feels designed."

The group / group-hover: pattern

This is Tailwind's most elegant compositional technique. It allows a parent element's hover state to control the styles of its children:

<!-- Without group: only hover on the icon itself triggers the icon colour change -->
<div>
  <div class="bg-gray-100 hover:bg-indigo-600">⚡</div>
  <h3>Frontend Engineering</h3>
</div>

<!-- With group: hovering anywhere on the card changes the icon colour -->
<div class="group hover:shadow-xl">
  <div class="bg-gray-100 group-hover:bg-indigo-600 transition-colors">⚡</div>
  <h3>Frontend Engineering</h3>
</div>

Tailwind generates CSS like .group:hover .group-hover\:bg-indigo-600 — a descendant selector. When the element with group is hovered, all its descendants with group-hover:* classes update.

Ring vs border — when to use which

  • border is part of the box model. It takes up space and affects layout. Adding a border changes the element's size.
  • ring is implemented with box-shadow. It renders outside (or inside) the element without affecting layout. It can be offset with ring-offset-*.
<!-- Featured card with a 2px ring at brand colour, offset from the element -->
<div class="ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2">
  <!-- The 2px ring sits outside the element with 2px white space between -->
</div>

Use border for structural card edges. Use ring for focus states, selected/featured indicators, and hover outlines that shouldn't affect layout.

transition-all for multi-property transitions

The service card uses transition-all duration-300 because multiple properties change on hover: border colour, shadow, and shadow colour. Rather than listing each individually, transition-all covers everything. Use it when 3+ properties transition simultaneously.

Hover shadow with colour and opacity

<div class="hover:shadow-xl hover:shadow-indigo-500/10">
  <!-- /10 means 10% opacity — very subtle glow, noticeable but not garish -->
</div>

Grand Archmage Solomon: "The featured card uses a ring, not a border. A border shifts the layout when added. A ring does not. The card does not jump when we highlight it. Details like this are what separate competent work from excellent work."

storyBeats.text: Sable the Illuminator is at the whiteboard. Three rectangles sketched out — cards, clearly — each with an icon, a heading, a description, a link. She taps the icon area.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: The services section must communicate value at a glance. Three cards. Clear hierarchy. And a hover that rewards attention. When the user hovers the card, the icon changes colour. Not because the icon is hovered — because the card is. This is the group pattern.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: The featured card uses a ring, not a border. A ring is implemented with box-shadow — it doesn't affect layout. Adding a border at render time would shift the card by 2px. A ring appears without displacing anything.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build the Arcane Guild's services section with three feature cards using the group/group-hover pattern, ring utilities for the featured card, and transition-all for multi-property hover effects.

  • .services: bg-slate-50, py-24, px-6
  • .services-grid: grid, grid-cols-1, md:grid-cols-3, gap-8
  • .service-card: bg-white, rounded-2xl, p-8, border, border-slate-200, hover:border-indigo-300, hover:shadow-xl, hover:shadow-indigo-500/10, transition-all, duration-300, group
  • .service-icon: w-12, h-12, bg-indigo-100, rounded-xl, flex, items-center, justify-center, text-2xl, mb-6, group-hover:bg-indigo-600, transition-colors, duration-300
  • .service-card--featured: inherits .service-card plus ring-2, ring-indigo-500, ring-offset-2

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a project card with image zoom and title reveal from scratch using group and group-hover:. The card shows an image placeholder (coloured div) that scales on hover, and a title that transitions from muted to full white. No class scaffold given — apply the group pattern without guidance.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Tailwind group / group-hover: pattern to a colleague who only knows basic hover states. Why can't you use a simple hover: variant on the child element (the icon) to achieve the same effect? Give a concrete example of where parent-driven hover control is necessary.

questions.prompt: How does the Tailwind group / group-hover: pattern work?
options: Adding group to a parent element allows its children to use group-hover: variants that activate when the parent (not the child) is hovered
group makes all children inherit the parent's hover state automatically without any additional classes
group-hover: is a shorthand for both the parent and child having the same hover:text-* class
group creates a CSS variable that child elements can read with var(--group-state)
questions.answer: Adding group to a parent element allows its children to use group-hover: variants that activate when the parent (not the child) is hovered
questions.explanation: Tailwind generates CSS like .group:hover .group-hover\:bg-indigo-600 — a descendant selector. When the element with group is hovered, all its descendants with group-hover:* classes update. This enables rich, coordinated hover effects across an entire card component.

questions.prompt: You have a card component that shows four properties changing on hover: border colour, shadow size, shadow colour, and background colour. Which transition utility is most appropriate?
options: transition-none — use CSS @keyframes instead for multiple properties
questions.explanation: When 3+ properties need to transition simultaneously, transition-all is the pragmatic choice — it covers every transitional property. transition (without -all) covers color, background-color, border-color, opacity, box-shadow, transform, filter, backdrop-filter — which also covers this case, but transition-all is more explicit when you want everything.

questions.prompt: You need to highlight a selected card among a grid of cards, adding a 2px indigo outline without shifting the other cards or causing layout reflow. Which approach is correct?
options: ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2 — ring uses box-shadow which does not affect layout
border-2 border-indigo-500 — add a 2px border to the selected card
outline-2 outline-indigo-500 — outline is always outside the box
shadow-indigo-500 shadow-md — use a coloured shadow as a border substitute
questions.answer: ring-2 ring-indigo-500 ring-offset-2 — ring uses box-shadow which does not affect layout
questions.explanation: Tailwind's ring-* utilities use box-shadow rather than border. Box-shadow does not affect the box model — it renders outside the element without pushing other elements around. Adding a ring to a selected card does not change its size or shift neighbouring cards. A border would change the element's rendered dimensions.
